entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m -q --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

# /loop
Parse input as `[interval] <prompt>`: a first token matching ^\d+[smhd]$ is the interval; else a trailing `every <N> <unit>` (only when a time follows "every"); else no interval (dynamic). Empty prompt → print `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.

## Fixed interval
Cron: Nm≤59 → `*/N * * * *`; Nm≥60 or Nh → `0 */H * * *`; Nd → `0 0 */N * *`; Ns → round up to minutes. Round uneven intervals to the nearest clean one and say so. CronCreate (recurring: true), confirm cadence + job ID in one line (expires after 7 days; cancel with CronDelete), then run the prompt now.

1. Run the prompt now (slash command → Skill tool).

The catalogue is complete now, and I've recorded what it says. The gateway lists seven aliases over three models.

| Alias | Served by | Context | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `engineering/b0`, `lead` | lead pool (Qwen3.6-35B) | 65,536 | off |
| `engineering/lead-reasoning` | lead pool | 65,536 | on |
| `engineering/deep` | deep pool (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next) | 65,536 | on |
| `engineering/interactive` | lead and deep pools | 65,536 | off |
| `engineering/interactive-rocm` | new host (qwen3-coder-30b) | 16,384 | off |
| `engineering/auto` | all three pools | 16,384 | off |

- **Release measurement is unaffected.** `deep` and `lead-reasoning` are each served by a single worker.
- **`auto` and `interactive` can be answered by more than one model.** A result on either isn't a result for one model unless each response's model is recorded.
- **`auto` is the CLI's configured default here and advertises a 16,384-token context**, a quarter of the other routes. That is worth knowing for everyday use; I haven't changed anything.
- **Not re-tested:** I read the catalogue once and sent no completions, so which model actually answers each alias is still unmeasured.

The evidence file and the v1.2.2 notes now carry this. That moved #683 to head `c1fcafa6` and restarted its checks at 20:21.

## Runner-like suite
The second full run finished with no product defect. Every failure was an eval test that fails the same way without the extra environment on this host:
- **Most of them:** the checkout here is group-writable, and the eval harness refuses a group-writable helper script. Removing that permission on the one file made `eval_integrity` pass 33 of 33 and `eval_hardened` 17 of 17.
- **`eval_version_probe_storage`:** needs a workspace fixture that only CI configures.

## Next
When #683's three checks pass at `c1fcafa6` and `main` is green, I'll merge it, wait for `main`'s CI on the merge commit, then tag a signed `v1.2.2-rc.1`. The watch is armed, with a fallback check at 20:41.

5:## After the stable tag
7:The release workflow does not touch the README, the CHANGELOG or `docs/releases/LATEST`. Once the stable tag is published, make a manual follow-up commit (a normal PR) that:
9:1. Sets `docs/releases/LATEST` to the new stable tag (one line, `vX.Y.Z`).
10:2. Updates the README status line ("the latest stable release is ...") and the README and `quickstart.md` install pins to that tag, and removes any "in development" wording for it.
11:3. Replaces `Unreleased` in the CHANGELOG heading of the new version with the tag date.

- name: Build desired managed UFW rule sets
  ansible.builtin.set_fact:
    security_ufw_management_rules: []
    security_ufw_inference_rules: []

- name: Build desired managed SSH UFW rules
  ansible.builtin.set_fact:
    security_ufw_management_rules: >-
      {{
        security_ufw_management_rules
        + [
          {
            'scope': 'management',
            'src': item,
            'port': '22',
            'proto': 'tcp',
            'comment': 'Managed SSH access'
          }
        ]
      }}
  loop: "{{ security_management_cidrs }}"

- name: Build desired managed inference UFW rules
  ansible.builtin.set_fact:
  when:
    - security_manage_runtime | bool
    - security_manage_sysctl | bool

- name: Allow SSH only from configured management CIDRs
  community.general.ufw:
    rule: allow
    port: "{{ item.port }}"
    proto: "{{ item.proto }}"
    src: "{{ item.src }}"
    comment: "{{ item.comment }}"
  loop: "{{ security_ufw_management_rules | default([]) }}"
  when:
    - security_manage_runtime | bool
    - security_firewall_enabled | bool

- name: Allow inference API only from configured CIDRs

# Project Guidelines & Agent Instructions

## Commands
- Environment Setup: `make bootstrap-tools` (manages `.venv`, pip hashes, galaxy requirements)
- Test: `.venv/bin/pytest -q` or `make test`
  - Target specific tests during development: `.venv/bin/pytest tests/unit/ -v` or `.venv/bin/pytest tests/test_observability_as_code.py`
  - Avoid running unbounded full-suite tests without specifying targets, as container baseline harnesses can take >15 minutes.

  - Rebuild & sync dashboard templates: `python3 observability/tools/build_dashboards.py`

- **Template Synchronization**: When modifying Grafana dashboards, NEVER edit only the static JSON or only the Jinja2 template. Always run `python3 observability/tools/build_dashboards.py` to ensure `observability/grafana/dashboards/*.json` and `roles/observability/templates/*.json.j2` stay strictly synchronized.
- **Zero/Idle Fallbacks**: Metrics for inference, workers, and gateway telemetry can be sparse when idle. PromQL queries must provide fallbacks (e.g. `or vector(0)` or `or (0 * sum by (...) (aihost_worker_info))` or `label_replace(...)`) and specify meaningful `noDataText` to avoid displaying "No data" panels.

- **Inventory & Release Bumps**: When deploying gateway updates, ensure release identifiers in `inventory/production/hosts.yml` or host variables match the deployed artifacts.

## Code Conventions
- Maintain documentation integrity and keep existing comments.
- Always run targeted tests after making changes to verify correctness.
- Keep functions modular and clearly typed.

# /loop
Parse input as `[interval] <prompt>`: a first token matching ^\d+[smhd]$ is the interval; else a trailing `every <N> <unit>` (only when a time follows "every"); else no interval (dynamic). Empty prompt → print `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.

## Fixed interval
Cron: Nm≤59 → `*/N * * * *`; Nm≥60 or Nh → `0 */H * * *`; Nd → `0 0 */N * *`; Ns → round up to minutes. Round uneven intervals to the nearest clean one and say so. CronCreate (recurring: true), confirm cadence + job ID in one line (expires after 7 days; cancel with CronDelete), then run the prompt now.

## Dynamic
1. Run the prompt now (slash command → Skill tool).
2. If the next run waits on an event, arm one Monitor (timeout_ms 1800000) unless TaskList shows one running.

v1.2.2 is released. It was published at 23:59 UTC on 21 November as the latest stable: https://github.com/mikeholownych/nexus-code/releases/tag/v1.2.2

## What I verified before publishing
- **Release workflow:** succeeded on the signed, verified tag at `ce2c951e`.
- **Archive integrity:** it matches its published checksums, and the build attestations for the archive and the checksum file both verify.
- **Same build as the candidate:** the archive has the same 420 files as rc.1. Only the ten version-bearing files differ, including the two Rust binaries, which are rebuilt with the new version number. The TypeScript client is byte-identical to the one measured on rc.1.
- **Public install:** after publishing, a fresh install into a throwaway home with attestation required reports `1.2.2 (ce2c951e249d)`.

Not done, as with v1.2.1: the tool-call measurement was not repeated on the stable archive, and nothing here is external qualification.

## Still open
- **Docs follow-up, PR #693:** points the README status line, the install pins and the latest-release marker at v1.2.2, dates the CHANGELOG heading, and records the verification above. CI is running; I'll merge it when green.
- **`release/v1.3.0`:** I'll create it from `main` once #693 merges. In a PR against that branch, I'll add the branch rule to `AGENTS.md` and extend post-merge CI and CodeQL to cover it.
- **Open PRs from other lanes:** three v1.3.0-track PRs (#689, #691, #692) still target `main`. I asked in the claims log that they be held and retargeted to the release branch. If one merges into `main` before the branch exists, it will simply be part of the branch's starting point.

After that, v1.3.0 work starts in your order: PF-1, PF-2, GV-4, GV-3, VR-1.

A watch is on #693, with a fallback check at 00:30.

# /loop
Parse input as `[interval] <prompt>`: a first token matching ^\d+[smhd]$ is the interval; else a trailing `every <N> <unit>` (only when a time follows "every"); else no interval (dynamic). Empty prompt → print `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.

## Fixed interval
Cron: Nm≤59 → `*/N * * * *`; Nm≥60 or Nh → `0 */H * * *`; Nd → `0 0 */N * *`; Ns → round up to minutes. Round uneven intervals to the nearest clean one and say so. CronCreate (recurring: true), confirm cadence + job ID in one line (expires after 7 days; cancel with CronDelete), then run the prompt now.

v1.2.2 has fully landed: it is published, `main` marks it as the latest stable, and `release/v1.3.0` now exists.

## Done
- **Docs follow-up #693 merged** (`main` at `550c6968`). Its checks passed against the current `main`, and `main` was green.
- **`release/v1.3.0` created** from that commit.
- **The two open PRs from other lanes (#689, #691) retargeted** to the release branch. I changed only their base.
- **Housekeeping:** my release claims are released and my scratch worktrees and branches removed. I kept the measurement inputs and outputs, and the downloaded stable assets, under `~/nexus-wt/`.

## One item left
**PR #694, against `release/v1.3.0`**, is waiting on CI. It contains:
- The release-branch rule in `AGENTS.md`: all work lands on `release/v<major>.<minor>.<patch>`, nothing merges into `main` until the release is ready to tag, and branches are brought up to date by merging, never by rebase or force-push.
- Post-merge CI and CodeQL extended to cover `release/**` branches.

This PR is also the first test of the setup, since its checks have to run against the new base. I'll merge it when the three required checks pass, then stop the loop.

## Corrections and notes
- **Correction to my last message:** Codex had taken a claim on the docs branch before rebasing it, so I was wrong that it worked without one. The force-push itself still broke the rule. I corrected the note in the claims log.
- **Branch protection:** `release/v1.3.0` has no protection rules that I set. If `main` has required checks enforced in GitHub settings, you may want the same on `release/**`. That is a repository setting, so I've left it to you.

Next is v1.3.0 in your order (PF-1, PF-2, GV-4, GV-3, VR-1), plus sunsetting the Cloudflare contest work. A watch is on #694, with a fallback check at 01:36.

- **v1.2.2:** published as the latest stable at 23:59 UTC on 21 November, from a signed and verified tag. `main` (`550c6968`) marks it as latest in the README, install pins and CHANGELOG.
- **`release/v1.3.0`:** created from that commit. PR #694 is merged into it, so `AGENTS.md` now carries the release-branch rule.
- **CI on the release branch:** post-merge CI and CodeQL now trigger on `release/**`. Both started on the merge commit (`128bd6bb`), which confirms the trigger works. I haven't read their results, since they had only just started.
- **The rule is already in use:** another lane merged its retargeted PR (#691) into `release/v1.3.0` rather than `main`.
- **My footprint:** I hold no claims, and my worktrees and branches for this release are removed. The only claim directories still carrying my name are archived handoff and reconciliation records from earlier in the day.

## Worth knowing from the release
- **Tool-call measurement on rc.1:** 200 of 200 on both `engineering/deep` and `engineering/lead-reasoning`, in one run. It was not repeated on the stable archive, and the gateway's new third model was not measured.
- **Defect found before tagging:** a failing type-check was treated as "could not run" when `FORCE_COLOR=1` was set. The fix shipped in v1.2.2.
- **Signing:** commits and tags in this repository now use the aisyndicate.io address, so they show as verified. Older commits stay unverified.
- **External PR:** vercel-labs/skills #2638 has verified commits now and is waiting on Vercel's own review.

## For you to decide
- **Branch protection on `release/**`:** I set none. If `main`'s required checks are enforced in GitHub settings, the release branch needs the same there.
- **Force-push by another session:** Codex rebased and force-pushed the docs branch once. The content was unchanged, and the new `AGENTS.md` section now states the rule explicitly.

Next up is v1.3.0 on the release branch, in your order: PF-1, PF-2, GV-4, GV-3, VR-1, then sunsetting the Cloudflare contest work. Say the word and I'll start with PF-1.

1	# Nexus Code v1.3 plan: the platform track
2	
3	Status: PLAN, written 2026-11-15 against `main` plus the v1.2.0-rc.1 notes, at the owner's request ("draft the v1.3 platform track as recommended"). It follows v1.2.1 and v1.2.2 ([`docs/v1.2.1/PLAN.md`](../v1.2.1/PLAN.md), decision D12). Nothing here is a claim that Nexus Code is frontier-grade, and no unit starts without the decisions in section 7.
4	
5	## 1. Purpose and theme
6	
7	Frontier clients are platforms: a CLI plus a desktop app, IDE integration, background and scheduled agents, an SDK or managed API, installable plugin bundles, and enterprise policy (web sources of 2026-11-15, mostly third-party; see [`docs/v1.2.1/GAP_ANALYSIS.md`](../v1.2.1/GAP_ANALYSIS.md) §2). Nexus is a single-binary Linux CLI and TUI. It cannot match breadth or first-party model fit, and a worse copy of three funded platforms is not a goal.
8	
9	The v1.3 theme: **let other programs drive Nexus and let teams govern it, without weakening the gate.** Every new surface (an IDE over ACP, a scheduler, a hook, a plugin, an SDK caller, a managed policy) goes through the same approval and verification gates as the terminal does. The differentiator to build on is the one nobody else ships by default: a completion you can audit (independent verification, receipts, evidence). Two consequences shape the plan:
10	
11	1. **Nexus as the verification layer for other harnesses.** `nexus verify` and an MCP/ACP `verify` tool let a Codex, Claude Code or Aider session ask Nexus to independently check its work. This costs little (the machinery exists) and is positioned where the platforms are weakest.
12	2. **Governance as a product.** Managed policy with fixed precedence, a hash-chained and optionally signed audit export, and hooks that can only tighten.
13	
14	Non-goals: a marketplace, a desktop or mobile app, a Nexus-specific VS Code extension (ACP clients already exist), hosted or multi-tenant operation (dropped 2026-11-15, decision D8), plugin auto-update, any new runtime dependency without a decision.
15	
16	## 2. Evidence and its limits
17	
18	- **Nexus today** (read-only inventory, 2026-11-15; "present" means present in source or docs, nothing was run): sidecar/TUI protocol is NDJSON over the sidecar's stdio with `PROTOCOL_VERSION = 1`, an event `v`, a one-way `hello`, typed unions in `cli/src/protocol.ts:53-204` hand-mirrored in `core/src/bin/nexus_tui/protocol.rs`, **no schema file, no socket**; `nexus run --json` returns `TaskExecutionResult` (`cli/src/core/app.ts:44`) with no schema or version, exit codes defined only in code (0 verified, 2 completed-unverified, 130 interrupted, 1 otherwise); `ApplicationCore` is an accidental re-export (`cli/src/index.ts:1240`) and `cli/package.json` has `main` and `bin` but no `exports` or `types`; operations are durable and resumable (per-operation lock, 12 h wait survives restart, `maxConcurrentUnits` capped at 64 and clamped to 1 without `git.isolate`) but **foreground-only**, with no scheduler, cron, trigger or daemon in the code; plugins are plain JS modules with no manifest, checksum or install command, workspace plugins load after `nexus trust` with full process authority, hooks cover pre/post tool only; policy is the workspace-local `.nexus-security.json`, **fails open to defaults on a parse error**, with no system or admin layer; session export is `nexus-session-export/2` reachable only through `/export`; the flight log is append-only by convention (no hash chain found) and the CERI evidence store hashes files but has no signature or verify command; local OTLP-style traces are written on every session with no opt-in gate and no network exporter found; a goal (objective ledger) persists across sessions via `--resume`, but nothing re-launches a task on its own.
19	- **Peers, read from source** (shallow clones of 2026-11-13/14; Codex at commit 336b19a; untrusted code, nothing run): ACP servers in goose (`crates/goose/src/acp`), Cline (`apps/cli/src/acp/acpAgent.ts`), Gemini CLI (`packages/cli/src/acp`) and opencode (`packages/cli/src/acp/agent.ts`), the Codex `app-server` (JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio, websocket or UDS; schema generated from Rust types and checked in); schedulers in goose (`scheduler/full.rs`), Cline (`*.cron.md` and event specs) and opencode (a `ScheduleTable` with `in`/`at`/`every`/`cron` and an optional deterministic wake `check`); hooks in Gemini CLI (`docs/hooks/reference.md`), goose (`hooks/mod.rs`), Cline and Codex; extension manifests in Gemini CLI (`gemini-extension.json`), goose (Open Plugins and Gemini formats) and opencode; policy tiers in Gemini CLI (`core/src/policy/config.ts:67-71`), opencode (`managed-policy.ts`) and Codex (`requirements.toml`); goal state in opencode (`schema/src/goal.ts`) and Codex (`thread/goal/*`).
20	- **XERJ reference queries** (2026-11-15, local node, read-only; the `opencode` index is flagged "not verified complete", so a miss there is not proof of absence): `xerj code opencode` for ACP, scheduling and plugin manifests; `xerj search --prefix goose` for ACP, scheduler and extension manifests; `xerj search --prefix xc-opencode` for managed policy. **Took:** opencode's wire-level ACP fixture pattern (`packages/cli/test/acp/wire-fixture.ts`) for protocol conformance tests; opencode's schedule model (`schema/src/schedule.ts`, `core/src/schedule/sql.ts`: `next_due_at`, `remaining_runs`, `last_outcome`, deterministic wake check with hard limits) and its documented GitHub scheduled-workflow example; goose's cron-on-a-recipe scheduler shape (`scheduler/full.rs`, `commands/schedule.rs`); goose's checked-in ACP schema and method metadata (`acp-meta.json`); goose's plugin formats (`plugins/formats/gemini.rs`, `open_plugins.rs`); opencode's managed policy as config statements with an action, a resource and an effect (`config/plugin/policy.ts`). **Rejected:** opencode's in-process Effect plugin hooks (a JS-in-process model is what Nexus is trying to move away from), goose's per-run `Auto` mode for scheduled runs (unattended runs must never get allow-always), and any code copied verbatim: reference code is read-only inspiration.
21	- **Research notes** (2026-11-15): the Anthropic 2026 agentic coding trends report (read in full; a vendor document with no methodology, customer-reported figures) and OpenHands (documentation, not source) support three priorities here: VR-1 and VR-2 (the report's own evidence is that people delegate what is cheaply checkable, so verifiability is the delegation boundary), PA-1 (it names a view of concurrent agent sessions) and AC-1 (above). They are framing, not evidence about Nexus.
22	- **Not covered:** Claude Code and agy were not read (web sources only); parts of Cline's daemon, Codex's hook handler types and plugin manifest, and goose's managed policy were sampled, not read in full; peer behaviour under load was not measured.
23	
24	## 3. Principles
25	
26	1. **Protocol first.** Nothing else in this plan is safe to build until the client protocol is published, schema'd, versioned and conformance-tested.
27	2. **One gate.** A new surface can request an approval but can never answer one on behalf of Nexus's own gates (SI-2, CS-* rules, verification). A client that answers "allow" to a denied action must have no effect; this is tested.
28	3. **Tighten only.** Hooks and managed policy may deny, require a human, or rewrite arguments toward safer values. They never grant.
29	4. **Unattended means stricter.** Scheduled and detached runs never get allow-always, run in a fresh worktree, and record that they were unattended in every receipt.
30	5. **Explicit trust.** Project-defined hooks, plugins and policy run only after a trust decision keyed by a content hash; a changed file asks again.
31	6. **Schemas come from types.** Generate JSON Schema from the TypeScript types and check it in with a parity test, so the Rust mirror cannot drift (reference: Codex `app-server-protocol` schema export, goose `acp-schema.json`).
32	7. **No new runtime dependency** without a decision. ACP is plain JSON-RPC; hash chains and ed25519 signing use `node:crypto`.
33	8. **Experimental is a flag.** New methods sit behind `experimental` at `initialize` (reference: Codex `experimentalApi`) until a conformance suite has run against two real clients.
34	
35	## 4. Workstreams and units
36	
37	Size: S = one PR; M = two to four PRs; L = a program. P0 = prerequisite, P1 = core, P2 = stretch.
38	
39	### PF: protocol and embedding foundation
40	
41	| Unit | What | Accept | Size | Pri |
42	|---|---|---|---|---|
43	| PF-1 | Publish the client protocol: JSON Schema generated from `cli/src/protocol.ts`, a checked-in copy, a TS/Rust parity test replacing hand-sync, capability negotiation in `hello` / `initialize` (version range, `experimental` flag), `docs/PROTOCOL.md`; wire-level conformance fixtures (reference: opencode `packages/cli/test/acp/wire-fixture.ts`) | schema diff fails CI when a type changes without a version decision; a recorded session replays through the fixture harness | M | P0 |
44	| PF-2 | `nexus run --json` result schema with a `schema_version`, documented exit codes in the manual, `--input-json` or stdin for the task | schema validated in tests; a consumer test parses the output | S | P0 |
45	| PF-3 | Transport beyond a parent's stdio: a unix domain socket (default) with a token and origin check for any localhost HTTP/WebSocket listener (reference: goose `acp/transport/auth.rs`, constant-time compare); several clients may attach and reattach | a second client attaches to a running session; a wrong token is refused; the socket is mode 0600 | M | P1 |
46	| PF-4 | Library entry point: a `lib` entry that does not run commander on import, `exports` and `types` in `cli/package.json`, a package name decision, a documented minimal embedding example that spawns the sidecar | an example script runs a verified task through the entry point in CI | M | P1 |

51	|---|---|---|---|---|
52	| AC-1 | ACP adapter over the sidecar protocol (stdio), hand-rolled JSON-RPC with no dependency: `initialize` with a capability list, `session/new`, `session/load`, `session/prompt`, `session/cancel`; streaming `tool_call` and `tool_call_update` with diff content; a `verification` update carrying receipt ids and verifier results; client-bound `session/request_permission` with allow-once and reject only (no "allow always" at first); one extension, `_nexus/receipt/get`. The host side exists too: OpenHands' Agent Canvas drives Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI and OpenCode over ACP (docs, 2026-11-15), so an ACP server is what makes Nexus drivable by such hosts | a scripted ACP client completes a task; an `allow` reply to an action the gates deny has no effect (gate test G-3); the receipt is retrievable | L | P1 |
53	| AC-2 | ACP conformance: fixture suite plus runs against two real ACP clients (decision D14), recorded as fixtures; no live model | both clients complete the basic flow; fixtures committed | M | P1 |

58

60	|---|---|---|---|---|
61	| VR-1 | `nexus verify` (no agent run): given a worktree or a base and head, run the discovered or configured verifier, the type-check evidence (CG-4), the verification-file guard and the independent reviewer, and print a verdict VERIFIED / REGRESSION_FREE / UNVERIFIED / BLOCKED with the receipt; exit code per the documented contract; usable as a CI gate (pairs with the v1.2.1 GitHub Action, RD-4) | a known-bad diff (weakened test) is not VERIFIED; the same diff produced by another harness gives the same verdict | M | P1 |
62	| VR-2 | Expose verification as an MCP tool and an ACP extension so another harness can call Nexus to check its own work (`serve-mcp` today exposes workspace tools, not verification); the caller can read the verdict but cannot change it | an external client's session gets a verdict and a receipt id; tampering with the request cannot raise the verdict | M | P1 (decision D20) |

67	|---|---|---|---|---|

70	| BG-3 | Event triggers (file change, webhook) | deferred: needs a trust and abuse model first | M | P2 (v1.4) |

74	| Unit | What | Accept | Size | Pri |
75	|---|---|---|---|---|
76	| GV-1 | Managed policy with fixed precedence **system > user > project**: `/etc/nexus/policy.toml` (path per decision D16), `~/.config/nexus/policy.toml`, then the existing `.nexus-security.json`; restrict-only semantics (deny, require a human, disable auto/yolo, allowlist MCP servers and plugins, set verification-path modes); the effective tier is printed beside every decision; a parse error in the system or user tier **fails closed**; a project policy file is hashed and a changed one asks again (reference: Gemini CLI tiers, MATCH/MISMATCH/NEW integrity check and system settings paths; opencode managed policy; Codex `requirements.toml`) | a project policy cannot loosen a system policy; a corrupted system policy refuses to start with a clear message instead of failing open; precedence table covered by tests | M | P1 |
77	| GV-2 | Audit export: `nexus audit export <task\|session>` writes a bundle (session export, receipts, evidence, verification attempts, flight log excerpt) with a manifest of SHA-256 hashes and a hash chain, optionally signed with an operator-provided ed25519 key (`node:crypto`, decision D17); `nexus audit verify` | a bundle with one altered byte fails verification and names the file; an unsigned bundle verifies by hash only and says so | M | P1 |
78	| GV-3 | Hash-chain the flight recorder and the verification-attempt log (today append-only by convention only) and verify the chain on `nexus flights replay` | truncating or editing a record is detected | S | P1 |
79	| GV-4 | Telemetry transparency (this also settles v1.2.1 unit PC-5): document what the local traces contain, add a setting to disable them and a retention limit, state plainly that nothing leaves the host (no network exporter found) | doc plus a test that no network call is made | S | P1 |

Project-defined hooks need a trust decision keyed by a hash of the command (reference: Gemini CLI `trusted_hooks.json`, goose `hooks/mod.rs`, Codex hook trust). Handler types: command only (no peer shipped http, prompt or subagent handlers in what was read) | a hook that returns `allow` for a denied action has no effect; a changed project hook asks again; the contract is documented so existing hook scripts of that shape transfer | M | P1 |
87	| HK-2 | Plugin manifest `nexus-plugin.json` (name, version, declared contributions: hooks, skills, verifiers, MCP servers; required permissions); install from a local path or a git URL **pinned to a commit hash**; capabilities shown at install, resolved commit recorded in an install receipt; `nexus plugins install\|list\|remove\|verify`; no marketplace and no auto-update (reference: Gemini CLI `gemini-extension.json`, goose `.goose-plugin-install.json`). Skills load on a declared trigger and are not always-on (references: OpenHands trigger-based skills, the on-demand-loading guidance of `agent-rules-books`). Also fix the documented example in `docs/SKILLS_AND_PLUGINS.md` that does not match the code (`onTurnStart` positional arguments versus a context object) and stop swallowing plugin load errors silently | installing a plugin whose declared permissions exceed the system policy is refused; `verify` detects a modified install; a skill whose trigger did not fire adds nothing to the request (request-shape snapshot) | M | P1 |
88	| HK-3 | Per-plugin trust instead of per-directory, and run workspace-defined plugin hooks as subprocesses rather than in-process (a trusted workspace today runs every `.js` file in it with full process authority) | decision D18; migration note for existing plugins | M | P2 |
89	
90	### PA: parallel agents and goals
91	
92	| Unit | What | Accept | Size | Pri |
93	|---|---|---|---|---|
94	| PA-1 | Parallel run visibility: `nexus operation watch` (CLI view first) showing units, worktrees and owners; a worktree owner id recorded in the receipt (reference: Codex `worktree` crate `owner` and `bind_thread`); a concurrency cap tied to a CPU and memory budget instead of a count only | two parallel units show their owners and states; the cap refuses a third when the budget is exhausted | M | P1 |
95	| PA-2 | Verified merge arbitration: when parallel units integrate, apply each diff, run verification on the merged tree, reject on failure. No peer read does more than isolate; this is where Nexus can differ | two units whose changes conflict semantically (each passes alone) fail verification on the merged tree and neither is integrated silently | M | P1 |
96	| PA-3 | Goal semantics: a ledger entry active from an earlier process resumes **paused** (opencode `goal.ts` boot id), stall counting by failure fingerprint and not turn count, completion decided only by a verifier receipt, an optional token budget rolling up from sub-operations (reference: Codex goal budget); `/team` leaves experimental only after PA-1 and PA-2 | stale goal resumes paused with a visible reason; a model "I am done" does not complete a goal | M | P2 |
97	| PA-4 | **Bounded delegation and workflow commands** (trail 428; [baseline](PA4_BASELINE.md)): extend transient `spawn_subagent` and durable operations with a shared validated delegation contract/outcome, enforce authority intersection and recursive/resource limits, then expose real `/goal`, `/loop`, and `/batch` lifecycles through REPL and TUI/sidecar. Reuse `TeamOrchestrator`, `ConvergenceScheduler`, `OperationStore`, `ResourceRegistry`, specialist profiles, provider recovery, completion evidence, and existing stagnation detectors; do not add a second scheduler or workflow store. `/goal` owns an immutable objective and requirement/evidence ledger; `/loop` is bounded and verifier-driven; `/batch` validates a task graph and maps it into existing work units. Parsing, cancellation, pause/resume, status, recovery, and provider-neutral fixtures are part of each command contract. Spec-format validation may proceed independently; lifecycle and shared-contract work depends on PA-1/PA-2 evidence and WP-P10-02, with `/goal` semantics aligned to PA-3. | prompt-only subagent compatibility; parent/profile/session authority intersection and enforced recursive limits; typed non-success and unknown-effect outcomes; each command has durable state, lifecycle controls, recovery and status through supported interfaces; dependency and workspace conflicts cannot silently complete or overwrite; deterministic verifiers and independent review gate acceptance; standard-contract mock plus existing local/cloud fixtures pass without provider changes | L (staged packages) | P1 |

99	## 5. Sequencing
100	
101	Phase A (foundation, parallelisable): PF-1, PF-2, GV-4, VR-1, GV-3. These unblock the rest and cost little.
102	Phase B: AC-1, HK-1, GV-1, GV-2, PF-4, PA-2, VR-2.
103	Phase C: BG-1, BG-2, HK-2, PF-3, AC-2, PA-1, GV-5.
104	Phase D (stretch, may roll to v1.4): PA-3, HK-3, BG-3.
105	PA-4 is staged: the existing operation-spec validator can be reused independently; command lifecycles and shared delegation changes follow WP-P10-02 and verified PA-1/PA-2 gates. `/goal` must also satisfy PA-3 before promotion.
106	
107	Dependencies on earlier plans: v1.2.1 RD-3 (`stream-json` output) feeds PF-2; RD-4 (GitHub Action) pairs with VR-1; CS-9 (per-command approval rules, v1.2.2) and GV-1 must agree on rule semantics (allow < prompt < forbidden, deciding rule recorded); MT-1 (the `agent.ts` split) makes AC-1 and BG-1 much easier and should land first if possible; PR-* (provider registry) is independent; MQ-* (measurement) should publish at least one result before this release claims anything.
108	
109	## 6. Release gates
110	
111	| Gate | Condition |
112	|---|---|
113	| G-1 | `make test` green at the exact head; required CI green; main CI green on the merge commit |
114	| G-2 | Protocol conformance: schema parity test and the wire-fixture suite green; AC-1 passes against two real clients or the release says "experimental" |
115	| G-3 | **Gate-bypass suite:** a hostile client, hook, plugin, schedule or policy file cannot approve a denied action, raise a verdict, widen a policy tier, or remove a verification-file protection |
116	| G-4 | Unattended runs: tests show no allow-always, a fresh worktree, the unattended flag in receipts, and a kill-and-resume pass |
117	| G-5 | Audit round trip: export, verify, tamper one byte, verify fails and names the file |
118	| G-6 | Docs and examples for every new surface (`docs/PROTOCOL.md`, hooks, plugins, policy, schedules, audit) with runnable examples in CI |
119	| G-7 | Notes keep the framing: "ledger closed, qualification pending" unless an external result (E2 per the v1.2.1 plan §7) exists |
120	
121	## 7. Decisions needed
122	
123	| Id | Decision | Default if unanswered |
124	|---|---|---|
125	| D13 | Publish an npm package or SDK (PF-4)? Package name and licence; external publishing is yours to authorise | no publish; the entry point is documented but not published |
126	| D14 | Which two ACP clients to test against (AC-2) | the two most widely used open-source ones that run on Linux without an account |
127	| D15 | Detached runner model: a documented `systemd --user` unit, or a self-daemonizing mode (BG-1) | the `systemd --user` unit only |
128	| D16 | System policy location and whether the system and user tiers fail closed on a parse error (GV-1) | `/etc/nexus/policy.toml`; fail closed |
129	| D17 | Audit signing: where the operator's ed25519 key lives and whether signing is required or optional (GV-2) | optional; key path supplied by the operator, never stored by Nexus |
130	| D18 | Whether in-process workspace JS plugins stay supported after HK-1/HK-2 (HK-3) | keep, but move to per-plugin trust with a deprecation note |
131	| D19 | Unattended-run defaults (BG-2): `read-only` only, or `worktree-write` allowed | `read-only` by default; `worktree-write` per schedule with an explicit flag |
132	| D20 | Position Nexus as a verifier for other harnesses (VR-2)? | yes |
133	| D21 | Event triggers and remote (SSH) execution: v1.4 or never | v1.4 candidate, no work in v1.3 |
134	
135	## 8. Risks
136	
137	| Risk | Mitigation |
138	|---|---|
139	| A new socket or listener widens the attack surface | unix socket mode 0600 by default; token and origin check for any HTTP listener; G-3 |
140	| A client answers approvals in a way that bypasses a gate | the gate decides first; the client only supplies a human's yes or no; G-3 tests it |
141	| Fail-closed policy locks an operator out | a clear message naming the file and tier, and a documented recovery path; tested |
142	| Unattended runs burn the shared gateway or contend with live measurements | schedules use the `GATEWAY` claim protocol; read-only default; run budget in every spec |
143	| Plugin supply chain | commit-pinned installs, capabilities shown, no auto-update, install receipt, `verify` |
144	| Protocol churn after publication | `experimental` flag, version range in `hello`, schema diff in CI |
145	| Scope: this track is as large as v1.2.0 plus v1.2.1 | the sequencing above; Phase D rolls without ceremony; a unit is never half-merged |
146	| An unreviewed peer assumption | sources and limits are listed in section 2; each unit's PR repeats the reference coding record (XERJ queries, what was taken or rejected) |

# Nexus Code v1.3 plan: the platform track

Status: PLAN, written 2026-11-15 against `main` plus the v1.2.0-rc.1 notes, at the owner's request ("draft the v1.3 platform track as recommended"). It follows v1.2.1 and v1.2.2 ([`docs/v1.2.1/PLAN.md`](../v1.2.1/PLAN.md), decision D12). Nothing here is a claim that Nexus Code is frontier-grade, and no unit starts without the decisions in section 7.

## 1. Purpose and theme

Frontier clients are platforms: a CLI plus a desktop app, IDE integration, background and scheduled agents, an SDK or managed API, installable plugin bundles, and enterprise policy (web sources of 2026-11-15, mostly third-party; see [`docs/v1.2.1/GAP_ANALYSIS.md`](../v1.2.1/GAP_ANALYSIS.md) §2). Nexus is a single-binary Linux CLI and TUI. It cannot match breadth or first-party model fit, and a worse copy of three funded platforms is not a goal.

The v1.3 theme: **let other programs drive Nexus and let teams govern it, without weakening the gate.** Every new surface (an IDE over ACP, a scheduler, a hook, a plugin, an SDK caller, a managed policy) goes through the same approval and verification gates as the terminal does. The differentiator to build on is the one nobody else ships by default: a completion you can audit (independent verification, receipts, evidence). Two consequences shape the plan:

1. **Nexus as the verification layer for other harnesses.** `nexus verify` and an MCP/ACP `verify` tool let a Codex, Claude Code or Aider session ask Nexus to independently check its work. This costs little (the machinery exists) and is positioned where the platforms are weakest.
2. **Governance as a product.** Managed policy with fixed precedence, a hash-chained and optionally signed audit export, and hooks that can only tighten.

Non-goals: a marketplace, a desktop or mobile app, a Nexus-specific VS Code extension (ACP clients already exist), hosted or multi-tenant operation (dropped 2026-11-15, decision D8), plugin auto-update, any new runtime dependency without a decision.

## 2. Evidence and its limits

- **Nexus today** (read-only inventory, 2026-11-15; "present" means present in source or docs, nothing was run): sidecar/TUI protocol is NDJSON over the sidecar's stdio with `PROTOCOL_VERSION = 1`, an event `v`, a one-way `hello`, typed unions in `cli/src/protocol.ts:53-204` hand-mirrored in `core/src/bin/nexus_tui/protocol.rs`, **no schema file, no socket**; `nexus run --json` returns `TaskExecutionResult` (`cli/src/core/app.ts:44`) with no schema or version, exit codes defined only in code (0 verified, 2 completed-unverified, 130 interrupted, 1 otherwise); `ApplicationCore` is an accidental re-export (`cli/src/index.ts:1240`) and `cli/package.json` has `main` and `bin` but no `exports` or `types`; operations are durable and resumable (per-operation lock, 12 h wait survives restart, `maxConcurrentUnits` capped at 64 and clamped to 1 without `git.isolate`) but **foreground-only**, with no scheduler, cron, trigger or daemon in the code; plugins are plain JS modules with no manifest, checksum or install command, workspace plugins load after `nexus trust` with full process authority, hooks cover pre/post tool only; policy is the workspace-local `.nexus-security.json`, **fails open to defaults on a parse error**, with no system or admin layer; session export is `nexus-session-export/2` reachable only through `/export`; the flight log is append-only by convention (no hash chain found) and the CERI evidence store hashes files but has no signature or verify command; local OTLP-style traces are written on every session with no opt-in gate and no network exporter found; a goal (objective ledger) persists across sessions via `--resume`, but nothing re-launches a task on its own.
- **Peers, read from source** (shallow clones of 2026-11-13/14; Codex at commit 336b19a; untrusted code, nothing run): ACP servers in goose (`crates/goose/src/acp`), Cline (`apps/cli/src/acp/acpAgent.ts`), Gemini CLI (`packages/cli/src/acp`) and opencode (`packages/cli/src/acp/agent.ts`), the Codex `app-server` (JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio, websocket or UDS; schema generated from Rust types and checked in); schedulers in goose (`scheduler/full.rs`), Cline (`*.cron.md` and event specs) and opencode (a `ScheduleTable` with `in`/`at`/`every`/`cron` and an optional deterministic wake `check`); hooks in Gemini CLI (`docs/hooks/reference.md`), goose (`hooks/mod.rs`), Cline and Codex; extension manifests in Gemini CLI (`gemini-extension.json`), goose (Open Plugins and Gemini formats) and opencode; policy tiers in Gemini CLI (`core/src/policy/config.ts:67-71`), opencode (`managed-policy.ts`) and Codex (`requirements.toml`); goal state in opencode (`schema/src/goal.ts`) and Codex (`thread/goal/*`).
- **XERJ reference queries** (2026-11-15, local node, read-only; the `opencode` index is flagged "not verified complete", so a miss there is not proof of absence): `xerj code opencode` for ACP, scheduling and plugin manifests; `xerj search --prefix goose` for ACP, scheduler and extension manifests; `xerj search --prefix xc-opencode` for managed policy. **Took:** opencode's wire-level ACP fixture pattern (`packages/cli/test/acp/wire-fixture.ts`) for protocol conformance tests; opencode's schedule model (`schema/src/schedule.ts`, `core/src/schedule/sql.ts`: `next_due_at`, `remaining_runs`, `last_outcome`, deterministic wake check with hard limits) and its documented GitHub scheduled-workflow example; goose's cron-on-a-recipe scheduler shape (`scheduler/full.rs`, `commands/schedule.rs`); goose's checked-in ACP schema and method metadata (`acp-meta.json`); goose's plugin formats (`plugins/formats/gemini.rs`, `open_plugins.rs`); opencode's managed policy as config statements with an action, a resource and an effect (`config/plugin/policy.ts`). **Rejected:** opencode's in-process Effect plugin hooks (a JS-in-process model is what Nexus is trying to move away from), goose's per-run `Auto` mode for scheduled runs (unattended runs must never get allow-always), and any code copied verbatim: reference code is read-only inspiration.
- **Research notes** (2026-11-15): the Anthropic 2026 agentic coding trends report (read in full; a vendor document with no methodology, customer-reported figures) and OpenHands (documentation, not source) support three priorities here: VR-1 and VR-2 (the report's own evidence is that people delegate what is cheaply checkable, so verifiability is the delegation boundary), PA-1 (it names a view of concurrent agent sessions) and AC-1 (above). They are framing, not evidence about Nexus.
- **Not covered:** Claude Code and agy were not read (web sources only); parts of Cline's daemon, Codex's hook handler types and plugin manifest, and goose's managed policy were sampled, not read in full; peer behaviour under load was not measured.

## 3. Principles

1. **Protocol first.** Nothing else in this plan is safe to build until the client protocol is published, schema'd, versioned and conformance-tested.
2. **One gate.** A new surface can request an approval but can never answer one on behalf of Nexus's own gates (SI-2, CS-* rules, verification). A client that answers "allow" to a denied action must have no effect; this is tested.
3. **Tighten only.** Hooks and managed policy may deny, require a human, or rewrite arguments toward safer values. They never grant.
4. **Unattended means stricter.** Scheduled and detached runs never get allow-always, run in a fresh worktree, and record that they were unattended in every receipt.
5. **Explicit trust.** Project-defined hooks, plugins and policy run only after a trust decision keyed by a content hash; a changed file asks again.
6. **Schemas come from types.** Generate JSON Schema from the TypeScript types and check it in with a parity test, so the Rust mirror cannot drift (reference: Codex `app-server-protocol` schema export, goose `acp-schema.json`).
7. **No new runtime dependency** without a decision. ACP is plain JSON-RPC; hash chains and ed25519 signing use `node:crypto`.
8. **Experimental is a flag.** New methods sit behind `experimental` at `initialize` (reference: Codex `experimentalApi`) until a conformance suite has run against two real clients.

## 4. Workstreams and units

Size: S = one PR; M = two to four PRs; L = a program. P0 = prerequisite, P1 = core, P2 = stretch.

### PF: protocol and embedding foundation

| Unit | What | Accept | Size | Pri |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PF-1 | Publish the client protocol: JSON Schema generated from `cli/src/protocol.ts`, a checked-in copy, a TS/Rust parity test replacing hand-sync, capability negotiation in `hello` / `initialize` (version range, `experimental` flag), `docs/PROTOCOL.md`; wire-level conformance fixtures (reference: opencode `packages/cli/test/acp/wire-fixture.ts`) | schema diff fails CI when a type changes without a version decision; a recorded session replays through the fixture harness | M | P0 |
| PF-2 | `nexus run --json` result schema with a `schema_version`, documented exit codes in the manual, `--input-json` or stdin for the task | schema validated in tests; a consumer test parses the output | S | P0 |
| PF-3 | Transport beyond a parent's stdio: a unix domain socket (default) with a token and origin check for any localhost HTTP/WebSocket listener (reference: goose `acp/transport/auth.rs`, constant-time compare); several clients may attach and reattach | a second client attaches to a running session; a wrong token is refused; the socket is mode 0600 | M | P1 |
| PF-4 | Library entry point: a `lib` entry that does not run commander on import, `exports` and `types` in `cli/package.json`, a package name decision, a documented minimal embedding example that spawns the sidecar | an example script runs a verified task through the entry point in CI | M | P1 |

### AC: ACP and IDE access

| Unit | What | Accept | Size | Pri |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| AC-1 | ACP adapter over the sidecar protocol (stdio), hand-rolled JSON-RPC with no dependency: `initialize` with a capability list, `session/new`, `session/load`, `session/prompt`, `session/cancel`; streaming `tool_call` and `tool_call_update` with diff content; a `verification` update carrying receipt ids and verifier results; client-bound `session/request_permission` with allow-once and reject only (no "allow always" at first); one extension, `_nexus/receipt/get`. Reference: goose, Cline, opencode, Gemini CLI ACP servers and the Codex app-server (all four ACP servers use the same three-option permission request; opencode attaches the diff to the request so the user decides with the change in view). The host side exists too: OpenHands' Agent Canvas drives Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI and OpenCode over ACP (docs, 2026-11-15), so an ACP server is what makes Nexus drivable by such hosts | a scripted ACP client completes a task; an `allow` reply to an action the gates deny has no effect (gate test G-3); the receipt is retrievable | L | P1 |
| AC-2 | ACP conformance: fixture suite plus runs against two real ACP clients (decision D14), recorded as fixtures; no live model | both clients complete the basic flow; fixtures committed | M | P1 |

This supersedes v1.2.1 unit RD-5 (ACP server mode), which moves here.

### VR: Nexus as the verification layer

| Unit | What | Accept | Size | Pri |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| VR-1 | `nexus verify` (no agent run): given a worktree or a base and head, run the discovered or configured verifier, the type-check evidence (CG-4), the verification-file guard and the independent reviewer, and print a verdict VERIFIED / REGRESSION_FREE / UNVERIFIED / BLOCKED with the receipt; exit code per the documented contract; usable as a CI gate (pairs with the v1.2.1 GitHub Action, RD-4) | a known-bad diff (weakened test) is not VERIFIED; the same diff produced by another harness gives the same verdict | M | P1 |
| VR-2 | Expose verification as an MCP tool and an ACP extension so another harness can call Nexus to check its own work (`serve-mcp` today exposes workspace tools, not verification); the caller can read the verdict but cannot change it | an external client's session gets a verdict and a receipt id; tampering with the request cannot raise the verdict | M | P1 (decision D20) |

### BG: background and scheduled runs

| Unit | What | Accept | Size | Pri |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| BG-1 | Detached runner: a user-level job runner that owns durable operations so a run survives its CLI process (decision D15: a documented `systemd --user` unit versus a self-daemonizing mode); foreground mode unchanged | kill the CLI, the run continues and resumes cleanly; the SI-7 kill test passes against the runner | L | P1 |
| BG-2 | Schedules: a spec (trigger `cron`, `every` or `once`; objective ledger id; `max_rounds`; timeout; policy `read-only` or `worktree-write`; optional deterministic wake `check` command with hard limits, reference opencode `schedule/check.ts:23-39`: 30 s, 20 tool calls, 32 KB, cannot create schedules or worktrees) stored beside operations (`next_due_at`, `remaining_runs`, `last_outcome` as in opencode `core/src/schedule/sql.ts`); `nexus schedule add\|list\|rm\|run-now`; each run in a fresh worktree; unattended flag in every receipt; no allow-always; delivery is a receipt plus a pointer file | a scheduled run on a seeded failing verifier ends BLOCKED and says so; an unattended run asking for approval is denied, not blocked forever; missed runs are reported, not silently skipped | L | P1 |
| BG-3 | Event triggers (file change, webhook) | deferred: needs a trust and abuse model first | M | P2 (v1.4) |

### GV: governance

| Unit | What | Accept | Size | Pri |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GV-1 | Managed policy with fixed precedence **system > user > project**: `/etc/nexus/policy.toml` (path per decision D16), `~/.config/nexus/policy.toml`, then the existing `.nexus-security.json`; restrict-only semantics (deny, require a human, disable auto/yolo, allowlist MCP servers and plugins, set verification-path modes); the effective tier is printed beside every decision; a parse error in the system or user tier **fails closed**; a project policy file is hashed and a changed one asks again (reference: Gemini CLI tiers, MATCH/MISMATCH/NEW integrity check and system settings paths; opencode managed policy; Codex `requirements.toml`) | a project policy cannot loosen a system policy; a corrupted system policy refuses to start with a clear message instead of failing open; precedence table covered by tests | M | P1 |
| GV-2 | Audit export: `nexus audit export <task\|session>` writes a bundle (session export, receipts, evidence, verification attempts, flight log excerpt) with a manifest of SHA-256 hashes and a hash chain, optionally signed with an operator-provided ed25519 key (`node:crypto`, decision D17); `nexus audit verify` | a bundle with one altered byte fails verification and names the file; an unsigned bundle verifies by hash only and says so | M | P1 |
| GV-3 | Hash-chain the flight recorder and the verification-attempt log (today append-only by convention only) and verify the chain on `nexus flights replay` | truncating or editing a record is detected | S | P1 |
| GV-4 | Telemetry transparency (this also settles v1.2.1 unit PC-5): document what the local traces contain, add a setting to disable them and a retention limit, state plainly that nothing leaves the host (no network exporter found) | doc plus a test that no network call is made | S | P1 |
| GV-5 | Admin controls from the system policy: a strict mode that disables auto and full-access, an MCP and plugin allowlist | strict mode refuses `--yes` and `--mode auto` with the policy source named | S | P1 |

### HK: hooks and plugins

| Unit | What | Accept | Size | Pri |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| HK-1 | Declarative command hooks: events `pre-tool`, `post-tool`, `pre-verify`, `post-verify`, `permission-request`, `session-start`, `session-end`, `stop`, `pre-compact`; JSON on stdin (`session_id`, `cwd`, `hook_event_name`, `tool_name`, `tool_input`) and on stdout (`decision`, `reason`, `hookSpecificOutput`), exit 2 blocks with stderr as the reason, a timeout, a scrubbed environment (reuse `buildMcpEnvironment`), results written to the receipt. A hook may only deny or tighten arguments, never grant (Gemini CLI also ignores `allow` from lower tiers). Project-defined hooks need a trust decision keyed by a hash of the command (reference: Gemini CLI `trusted_hooks.json`, goose `hooks/mod.rs`, Codex hook trust). Handler types: command only (no peer shipped http, prompt or subagent handlers in what was read) | a hook that returns `allow` for a denied action has no effect; a changed project hook asks again; the contract is documented so existing hook scripts of that shape transfer | M | P1 |
| HK-2 | Plugin manifest `nexus-plugin.json` (name, version, declared contributions: hooks, skills, verifiers, MCP servers; required permissions); install from a local path or a git URL **pinned to a commit hash**; capabilities shown at install, resolved commit recorded in an install receipt; `nexus plugins install\|list\|remove\|verify`; no marketplace and no auto-update (reference: Gemini CLI `gemini-extension.json`, goose `.goose-plugin-install.json`). Skills load on a declared trigger and are not always-on (references: OpenHands trigger-based skills, the on-demand-loading guidance of `agent-rules-books`). Also fix the documented example in `docs/SKILLS_AND_PLUGINS.md` that does not match the code (`onTurnStart` positional arguments versus a context object) and stop swallowing plugin load errors silently | installing a plugin whose declared permissions exceed the system policy is refused; `verify` detects a modified install; a skill whose trigger did not fire adds nothing to the request (request-shape snapshot) | M | P1 |
| HK-3 | Per-plugin trust instead of per-directory, and run workspace-defined plugin hooks as subprocesses rather than in-process (a trusted workspace today runs every `.js` file in it with full process authority) | decision D18; migration note for existing plugins | M | P2 |

### PA: parallel agents and goals

| Unit | What | Accept | Size | Pri |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PA-1 | Parallel run visibility: `nexus operation watch` (CLI view first) showing units, worktrees and owners; a worktree owner id recorded in the receipt (reference: Codex `worktree` crate `owner` and `bind_thread`); a concurrency cap tied to a CPU and memory budget instead of a count only | two parallel units show their owners and states; the cap refuses a third when the budget is exhausted | M | P1 |
| PA-2 | Verified merge arbitration: when parallel units integrate, apply each diff, run verification on the merged tree, reject on failure. No peer read does more than isolate; this is where Nexus can differ | two units whose changes conflict semantically (each passes alone) fail verification on the merged tree and neither is integrated silently | M | P1 |
| PA-3 | Goal semantics: a ledger entry active from an earlier process resumes **paused** (opencode `goal.ts` boot id), stall counting by failure fingerprint and not turn count, completion decided only by a verifier receipt, an optional token budget rolling up from sub-operations (reference: Codex goal budget); `/team` leaves experimental only after PA-1 and PA-2 | stale goal resumes paused with a visible reason; a model "I am done" does not complete a goal | M | P2 |

Reuse `TeamOrchestrator`, `ConvergenceScheduler`, `OperationStore`, `ResourceRegistry`, specialist profiles, provider recovery, completion evidence, and existing stagnation detectors; do not add a second scheduler or workflow store. `/goal` owns an immutable objective and requirement/evidence ledger; `/loop` is bounded and verifier-driven; `/batch` validates a task graph and maps it into existing work units. Parsing, cancellation, pause/resume, status, recovery, and provider-neutral fixtures are part of each command contract. Spec-format validation may proceed independently; lifecycle and shared-contract work depends on PA-1/PA-2 evidence and WP-P10-02, with `/goal` semantics aligned to PA-3. | prompt-only subagent compatibility; parent/profile/session authority intersection and enforced recursive limits; typed non-success and unknown-effect outcomes; each command has durable state, lifecycle controls, recovery and status through supported interfaces; dependency and workspace conflicts cannot silently complete or overwrite; deterministic verifiers and independent review gate acceptance; standard-contract mock plus existing local/cloud fixtures pass without provider changes | L (staged packages) | P1 |

Phase A (foundation, parallelisable): PF-1, PF-2, GV-4, VR-1, GV-3. These unblock the rest and cost little.
Phase B: AC-1, HK-1, GV-1, GV-2, PF-4, PA-2, VR-2.
Phase C: BG-1, BG-2, HK-2, PF-3, AC-2, PA-1, GV-5.
Phase D (stretch, may roll to v1.4): PA-3, HK-3, BG-3.
PA-4 is staged: the existing operation-spec validator can be reused independently; command lifecycles and shared delegation changes follow WP-P10-02 and verified PA-1/PA-2 gates. `/goal` must also satisfy PA-3 before promotion.

Dependencies on earlier plans: v1.2.1 RD-3 (`stream-json` output) feeds PF-2; RD-4 (GitHub Action) pairs with VR-1; CS-9 (per-command approval rules, v1.2.2) and GV-1 must agree on rule semantics (allow < prompt < forbidden, deciding rule recorded); MT-1 (the `agent.ts` split) makes AC-1 and BG-1 much easier and should land first if possible; PR-* (provider registry) is independent; MQ-* (measurement) should publish at least one result before this release claims anything.

## 6. Release gates

| Gate | Condition |
|---|---|
| G-1 | `make test` green at the exact head; required CI green; main CI green on the merge commit |
| G-2 | Protocol conformance: schema parity test and the wire-fixture suite green; AC-1 passes against two real clients or the release says "experimental" |
| G-3 | **Gate-bypass suite:** a hostile client, hook, plugin, schedule or policy file cannot approve a denied action, raise a verdict, widen a policy tier, or remove a verification-file protection |
| G-4 | Unattended runs: tests show no allow-always, a fresh worktree, the unattended flag in receipts, and a kill-and-resume pass |
| G-5 | Audit round trip: export, verify, tamper one byte, verify fails and names the file |
| G-6 | Docs and examples for every new surface (`docs/PROTOCOL.md`, hooks, plugins, policy, schedules, audit) with runnable examples in CI |
| G-7 | Notes keep the framing: "ledger closed, qualification pending" unless an external result (E2 per the v1.2.1 plan §7) exists |

## 7. Decisions needed

| Id | Decision | Default if unanswered |
|---|---|---|
| D13 | Publish an npm package or SDK (PF-4)? Package name and licence; external publishing is yours to authorise | no publish; the entry point is documented but not published |
| D14 | Which two ACP clients to test against (AC-2) | the two most widely used open-source ones that run on Linux without an account |
| D15 | Detached runner model: a documented `systemd --user` unit, or a self-daemonizing mode (BG-1) | the `systemd --user` unit only |
| D16 | System policy location and whether the system and user tiers fail closed on a parse error (GV-1) | `/etc/nexus/policy.toml`; fail closed |
| D17 | Audit signing: where the operator's ed25519 key lives and whether signing is required or optional (GV-2) | optional; key path supplied by the operator, never stored by Nexus |
| D18 | Whether in-process workspace JS plugins stay supported after HK-1/HK-2 (HK-3) | keep, but move to per-plugin trust with a deprecation note |
| D19 | Unattended-run defaults (BG-2): `read-only` only, or `worktree-write` allowed | `read-only` by default; `worktree-write` per schedule with an explicit flag |
| D20 | Position Nexus as a verifier for other harnesses (VR-2)? | yes |
| D21 | Event triggers and remote (SSH) execution: v1.4 or never | v1.4 candidate, no work in v1.3 |

## 8. Risks

| Risk | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| A new socket or listener widens the attack surface | unix socket mode 0600 by default; token and origin check for any HTTP listener; G-3 |
| A client answers approvals in a way that bypasses a gate | the gate decides first; the client only supplies a human's yes or no; G-3 tests it |
| Fail-closed policy locks an operator out | a clear message naming the file and tier, and a documented recovery path; tested |
| Unattended runs burn the shared gateway or contend with live measurements | schedules use the `GATEWAY` claim protocol; read-only default; run budget in every spec |
| Plugin supply chain | commit-pinned installs, capabilities shown, no auto-update, install receipt, `verify` |
| Protocol churn after publication | `experimental` flag, version range in `hello`, schema diff in CI |
| Scope: this track is as large as v1.2.0 plus v1.2.1 | the sequencing above; Phase D rolls without ceremony; a unit is never half-merged |
| An unreviewed peer assumption | sources and limits are listed in section 2; each unit's PR repeats the reference coding record (XERJ queries, what was taken or rejected) |

The detail behind the "Reference coding" rule in `AGENTS.md`: how to reach the local XERJ node, what to query, and what to leave alone.

- Before non-trivial code with a peer-project analogue (feature, protocol, parser, worktree or provider handling, tool, test harness), query the local XERJ node and record what you took, borrowed or rejected in the PR's 
- XERJ is an owner-host tool, not a project dependency (`docs/v1.1.0/DECISIONS.md` §1). Where it is unavailable (contributor machine, CI), write "XERJ unavailable: <reason>" in that section and use `git grep` plus the p
- The node is the user service `xerj` on `http://localhost:9200`; confirm with `systemctl --user is-active xerj` and use that node. Stop a hub with `xerj hub stop`.

- `nexus-cli`, `nexus-core`, `nexus-test`, `nexus-docs` index `origin/main` only (hourly), so open PRs are absent: use `git grep` on your branch.
- Reference code is read-only inspiration. Follow each result's licence tag; copy verbatim only permissively licensed code, with a citation. Keep XERJ and reference corpora away from held-out evaluation tasks (`docs/v1.0
- After real use: `xerj feedback --dry-run`, then `xerj feedback --submit --agent "<model>" --used-for "<task>" --verdict "<what worked and what did not>"`, with secrets and private data left out.

input.prompt:
You are implementing slice A of plan unit PF-1 in the nexus-code repository. Work ONLY in the git worktree `/home/mike/nexus-wt/pf1` (branch `v1/pf1-protocol-schema`, based on `origin/release/v1.3.0`). Read `/home/mike/nexus-wt/pf1/AGENTS.md` first and follow it.

## Goal
Publish the sidecar client protocol as a JSON Schema that is GENERATED from the TypeScript types in `cli/src/protocol.ts`, check the generated file in, and make drift fail the tests. Plan text (docs/v1.3.0/PLAN.md, PF-1): "JSON Schema generated from `cli/src/protocol.ts`, a checked-in copy ... schema diff fails CI when a type changes without a version decision". Slice A covers the generator, the checked-in schema, the drift check, and a version ledger. NOT in this slice: capability negotiation in `hello`, the Rust parity test, docs/PROTOCOL.md prose beyond a short README beside the schema, wire-fixture replay. Do not start those.

## What exists
- `cli/src/protocol.ts`: `PROTOCOL_VERSION = 1`, the unions `SidecarEvent` (sidecar to client) and `SidecarCommand` (client to sidecar). On the wire every message is one NDJSON line with an extra field `v` equal to the protocol version (see `encodeEvent` and `parseCommand`). Event types reference imported types (`TurnResult`, `ApprovalReview`, `SlashSpec`, `ReceiptSection`, `EvidenceStatus`, `Catalog`), which must be expanded into the schema.
- `cli/test/protocol_golden.test.ts` and `cli/test/fixtures/protocol_v1_golden.jsonl`: a small golden corpus shared with the Rust TUI.
- The repo uses TypeScript 7 (`cli/node_modules/typescript` 7.0.2). It has NO classic compiler API (`require('typescript').createProgram` is undefined). It does export `typescript/unstable/sync` (API, Program, Checker, TypeFlags, Symbol, isObjectType, isLiteralType, isIntersectionType, ...) and `typescript/unstable/ast`. I verified these load; I did not explore how to use them. Look under `cli/node_modules/typescript/{api,ast,lib}` for their typings and any README.

## Constraints (hard)
- No new dependency of any kind (no ajv, no ts-json-schema-generator, no second TypeScript). `cli/package.json` dependencies and the lockfile must not change.
- Generate from the types using the type checker. Preferred: `typescript/unstable/sync`. If, after a real attempt, that API cannot resolve the unions to their expanded property types, STOP and report exactly what failed and what you tried, with the smallest reproducer. Do not fall back to hand-writing the schema or to regex-parsing the source without telling me; a hand-written schema is not acceptable for this unit.
- The generator must be deterministic (stable key and variant order, no timestamps, no absolute paths) so its output can be compared byte for byte.
- Preserve existing comments and unrelated code. Do not edit `cli/src/protocol.ts` except if strictly needed (prefer not at all in this slice).
- Do not run `git commit`, `git push`, `gh`, or anything that publishes. Leave the changes uncommitted in the worktree for me to review.
- Tests: a throwaway HOME is mandatory, e.g. `cd /home/mike/nexus-wt/pf1/cli && HOME=$(mktemp -d) node --import tsx --test test/<name>.test.ts`. `cli/node_modules` may be missing in the worktree: copy it with `cp -a /home/mike/nexus-code/cli/node_modules /home/mike/nexus-wt/pf1/cli/node_modules` (do not run npm install). Type-check with `cd cli && npx tsc --noEmit`.
- Run everything in the foreground. No background jobs, no watcher or polling loops, no `sleep` loops, never `pkill -f`.
- Never print or read `~/.config/nexus/config.env`. No network calls.

## Deliverables
1. `cli/scripts/gen_protocol_schema.mjs` (or `.ts` run through `tsx`, your call; match how other scripts in `cli/scripts/` are written): generates JSON Schema draft 2020-12 for the wire protocol into `docs/protocol/sidecar-v1.schema.json`. Shape: top-level `$defs` with `SidecarEvent` and `SidecarCommand`, each a `oneOf` over the message variants discriminated by a `const` `type`; each variant an object schema with `required`, typed `properties` (including the wire field `v` as `const` PROTOCOL_VERSION), string-literal unions as `enum`, `null` unions, arrays, nested objects, and shared named types (TurnResult, ApprovalReview, ReceiptSection, Catalog and their members) emitted once under `$defs` and referenced with `$ref` where the checker gives you a named alias or interface. Carry JSDoc comments into `description` if the API makes that cheap; skip it if not. Decide `additionalProperties` deliberately and say why in the README: events must stay forward compatible (a newer sidecar may add optional fields that an older client ignores), so do not forbid extra properties on events.
   - `--check` mode: exit non-zero with a short message naming the file when the checked-in schema differs from a fresh generation.
2. The generated `docs/protocol/sidecar-v1.schema.json`, checked in, plus `docs/protocol/README.md` (short: what the file is, how to regenerate, the additionalProperties choice, that it is generated and must not be edited by hand).
3. A version ledger `docs/protocol/VERSIONS.json`: a list of entries `{ "protocol": 1, "schemaSha256": "<sha256 of the schema file>", "note": "..." }`, newest last. Rule to enforce in a test: the sha256 of the current checked-in schema must equal the LAST ledger entry's hash, and that entry's `protocol` must equal `PROTOCOL_VERSION`. So any type change forces a regenerated schema AND a new ledger entry, where the author records the decision (same version because the change is additive and compatible, or a bumped version). Explain this in the README in two or three sentences.
4. `cli/test/protocol_schema.test.ts` with at least:
   - the checked-in schema equals a fresh generation (drift);
   - the ledger rule above;
   - every record of `cli/test/fixtures/protocol_v1_golden.jsonl` validates against the schema for its direction, using a SMALL validator written in the test helper (support only the keywords your generator emits: type, const, enum, properties, required, items, oneOf/anyOf, $ref, additionalProperties). Put the validator in `cli/test/helpers/` so later slices can reuse it;
   - negative cases: a message with an unknown `type`, a missing required field, and a wrong-typed field are each rejected by the validator;
   - every `case "<type>"` handled by `parseCommand` appears as a command variant in the schema, and the reverse (so the parser and the type cannot drift apart silently).
   Check `cli/scripts/check_test_leaks.mjs` passes (`node scripts/check_test_leaks.mjs` from `cli/`) and that any new test file is picked up by the shard/tier scripts the way existing tests are (look at `cli/scripts/test_shards.mjs`, `test_tiers.mjs`, `test_durations.json`; if a new test must be registered somewhere, register it and tell me).
5. Wire the check into the existing flow only if there is an obvious existing place (for example a `check_*` step already run by `make test` or in `cli/package.json` scripts). If it needs a workflow-file change, do NOT edit `.github/workflows/*`; tell me instead. The test in item 4 already makes CI fail on drift, which is the acceptance criterion.

## Verify before reporting
- `npx tsc --noEmit` clean in `cli/`.
- The new test file passes; `protocol.test.ts`, `protocol_golden.test.ts`, `sidecar.test.ts` still pass.
- Show that drift is detected: temporarily add an optional field to one event variant in `cli/src/protocol.ts`, run the new test, confirm it FAILS, then revert the edit and confirm `git diff --stat cli/src/protocol.ts` is empty.
- Run the generator twice and confirm identical output.

## Report back (concise, facts only)
- Files added or changed (paths), and the generator's approach in a few sentences, including exactly which `typescript/unstable/*` calls it depends on and how fragile you judge that.
- Test results with pass/fail counts, and the drift demonstration outcome.
- Anything you could not do, any type the generator could not express and how it is represented instead (for example `any`, index signatures, intersections), and any decision you made that I should review.
- The schema's size (bytes, number of event and command variants).
Do not claim something works unless you ran it.
